name: Greek natural philosophy & medicine
summary: In the Greek cities of Ionia, southern Italy and Athens, thinkers began to explain the world through natural causes, argument and observation rather than myth. Hippocratic physicians treated disease as a natural process with natural remedies, and Aristotle built a vast system of physics, cosmology and biology that shaped European thought for two thousand years.

name: Hellenistic science & mathematics
summary: After Alexander's conquests, royal patronage in Alexandria, with its Museum and Library, made the city the capital of learning. Euclid set geometry in axiomatic form, Archimedes joined mathematics to mechanics, Eratosthenes measured the Earth and Hipparchus put astronomy on a quantitative footing. The Antikythera mechanism shows how far their technical skill could reach.

name: Roman & late-antique science
summary: Under Roman rule Greek remained the language of science. Ptolemy's astronomy and geography and Galen's medicine became the great summaries of ancient knowledge, authoritative for more than a millennium. Late-antique teachers such as Hypatia of Alexandria preserved and commented on these texts as the classical world faded.

name: Islamic science & the translation movement
summary: In Abbasid Baghdad and across the Islamic world, Greek, Persian and Indian works were translated into Arabic and then extended. Scholars developed algebra and Indian decimal numerals, a new experimental optics and a systematic medicine. From the twelfth century, translations from Arabic into Latin in Spain and Sicily carried this learning, and much of Greek science with it, into Europe. This tradition will have its own section.

name: Medieval Latin scholarship
summary: The new universities of Paris, Oxford and Bologna absorbed the translated works of Aristotle, Euclid, Ptolemy and their Arabic commentators. Scholars such as Roger Bacon and Nicole Oresme argued for mathematics and experience in natural knowledge, analysed motion and questioned whether the Earth stood still, while Fibonacci brought Hindu-Arabic arithmetic to European merchants.

name: Renaissance anatomy & astronomy
summary: Printing, the recovery of ancient texts and a new trust in direct observation transformed the study of the body and the heavens. Leonardo dissected and drew, Vesalius corrected Galen from the dissecting table, Copernicus set the Sun at the centre of the planetary system and Tycho Brahe built instruments of unprecedented precision.

name: Scientific Revolution
summary: In a few generations the Aristotelian picture of nature gave way to a mechanical, mathematical one. Kepler found the laws of planetary motion, Galileo turned the telescope on the sky and founded a mathematical science of motion, Harvey discovered the circulation of the blood, and the microscope revealed a hidden world. Scientific societies and journals made knowledge a public, shared enterprise.

name: The Newtonian age
summary: Newton's Principia united earthly and heavenly motion under one law of gravitation, and with Leibniz the calculus became the language of physics. Over the following decades Euler and others extended the new mathematics, while practical problems such as finding longitude at sea drove precision instrument-making.

name: Enlightenment chemistry & natural history
summary: The eighteenth century classified and measured. Linnaeus named the living world, Franklin showed lightning to be electrical, Lavoisier founded modern chemistry on careful weighing, Laplace extended Newtonian mechanics to the whole solar system, and Jenner's vaccine opened the age of preventive medicine. Humboldt's travels joined it all into a vision of nature as an interconnected whole.

name: Mathematics in the age of rigour
summary: Mathematicians rebuilt their subject on firmer foundations and pushed it into new territory. Gauss transformed number theory and geometry, Riemann reimagined space itself, Cantor created the theory of infinite sets, and new algebraic structures appeared that would later prove essential to physics.

name: Atoms & the periodic table
summary: Dalton revived the ancient idea of atoms as a precise chemical theory, with each element made of atoms of a characteristic weight. As more elements were found and their weights measured, chemists sought order among them, which Mendeleev found in the periodic table and used to predict elements still unknown.

name: Electromagnetism & classical physics
summary: Faraday's experiments revealed the intimate link between electricity and magnetism and gave the world the dynamo and the idea of the field. Maxwell expressed the whole subject in a set of equations and showed light to be an electromagnetic wave. Alongside this, the science of heat and energy, thermodynamics, took shape, and the century ended with the discovery of X-rays.

name: Geology, evolution & heredity
summary: Geologists showed the Earth to be immensely old and shaped by slow, ordinary processes. On that timescale Darwin and Wallace explained the diversity of life through natural selection, and Mendel's quiet experiments with peas found the rules of inheritance, overlooked until 1900.

name: Public health, germ theory & modern medicine
summary: Statistics and mapping revealed how disease spread, and the work of Pasteur and Koch proved that many diseases are caused by specific microbes. Antiseptic surgery, new vaccines and an understanding of the nervous system followed, and in the twentieth century the discovery of penicillin began the antibiotic era.

name: X-rays, radioactivity & the atom
summary: Within a few years of 1895, X-rays, radioactivity and the electron were discovered, and the indivisible atom of the chemists turned out to have structure. Marie Curie isolated new radioactive elements, Rutherford found the tiny atomic nucleus, and Bohr's quantum model of the atom explained the spectra of light that elements emit.

name: Relativity & quantum mechanics
summary: Two revolutions overturned Newtonian physics at its extremes. Planck's quantum and Einstein's relativity, special and general, changed the meaning of energy, space, time and gravity, and in the 1920s Heisenberg, Schrödinger and others built quantum mechanics, a theory of great predictive power whose interpretation is debated to this day.

name: Logic & the foundations of mathematics
summary: Logic was made into algebra and then into a precise language for all of mathematics. Hilbert hoped to secure mathematics completely through formal proof, but Gödel showed that any such system must leave some truths unprovable, and Turing's analysis of computation followed directly from the same questions.

name: Cosmology & the expanding universe
summary: General relativity made the shape and history of the universe a scientific question. Hubble showed that the spiral nebulae are galaxies far beyond our own and that they recede from us, and Lemaître proposed that the universe began in a hot, dense state, the idea later called the Big Bang.

name: Computing & information
summary: Babbage designed mechanical engines for calculation and Lovelace saw that they could manipulate any symbols, not only numbers. A century later Turing defined computation itself, wartime codebreaking and the first electronic computers made it real, and Shannon's theory of information gave the digital age its mathematics.

name: Genetics & molecular biology
summary: Physicists and chemists turned to the question of how heredity works at the level of molecules. X-ray crystallography revealed the double-helix structure of DNA in 1953, showing how genetic information is stored and copied, and the following decade worked out how that information is turned into proteins.
